solution_full: This is a Riemann sum for $f(x)=\log_e\dfrac{2x}{1+x}$ on $(0,1]$. The singularity of $\log_e x$ at $0$ is integrable and $f$ is increasing, so the sum converges to $\int_0^{1}f(x)\,dx$.
By continuity of the exponential function, $\lim P_n=e^{-\log_e2}=\dfrac12=0.50$.
originality_note: New: a product of the ratios 2k/(n+k), each tending to a different value, whose geometric mean tends to exactly 1/2 through cancellation of log integrals (way 4). Closest known: lim ((n+1)(n+2)...(2n)/n^n)^{1/n} = 4/e and lim prod (k/n)^{k/n^2} = e^{-1/4} (OEIS). Different because: the numerator and denominator logs cancel to give a rational limit. The first design (prod (k/n)^{k/n^2}) was replaced after the web check found it in OEIS A366271.
blueprint_concepts: Definite integral as the limit of a sum
Evaluation of limit involving exponential and logarithmic functions

concept_use.Definite integral as the limit of a sum: After taking logarithms the expression is a Riemann sum for int_0^1 log((2x)/(1+x)) dx.
concept_use.Evaluation of limit involving exponentia: The limit of the product is found from the limit of its logarithm, L = e^{lim log P_n}, a 1^infinity-type exponential/logarithmic limit.

stem_review: Read as a student: the product is explicit; the limit exists. Checked with the integral and numerically. Answer 0.50 lies between 0 and 1 as planned. Changed: redesigned after the web check (see originality note).
key_step: Take logs to get a Riemann sum of log(2x/(1+x)) and evaluate three log integrals.
justification: Two linked ideas: logarithm to turn a product limit into a Riemann sum, and the log integrals with an integrable singularity; numerical answer. Comparable to 2023-P2-Q8 (L3) in demand; standard for Advanced products.
